A Raspberry Pi costs less than most smartphones, but with the right hardware, it can receive signals from satellites, track aircraft flying overhead, and even control a telescope. It’s a tiny computer that people have turned into everything from home automation systems to custom scientific instruments. And most of these projects don’t require expensive equipment or years of programming experience.

What makes the Raspberry Pi interesting is how easily it connects to other hardware. Add a radio receiver, and you can pick up publicly transmitted aircraft data or weather satellite signals. Connect a camera, and it can run facial recognition software. Attach GPS hardware, and you’ve got the foundation for a navigation system you can build around your own needs. The Pi handles the computing while the additional components give it new capabilities.

A lot of technology that once required specialized equipment can now be built at home with affordable parts and open-source software. You still need to understand how the components work together, but there are already thousands of projects, tutorials, and communities dedicated to helping people figure that out. The Raspberry Pi has made it possible to experiment with technologies that most people would never think to build themselves.
